title: Central root-string brackets and integral half-sums after orienting a root pair
statement:
Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional split semisimple Lie algebra over $\mathbf Q$ [def-wf-lie-algebra], [def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra], with splitting Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ and reduced crystallographic root system $R\subset\mathfrak h^\vee$. Fix a Chevalley basis: $h_i$ are the simple coroots, the $e_\gamma$ are nonzero root vectors ($[h,e_\gamma]=\gamma(h)e_\gamma$ for $h\in\mathfrak h$), $[e_\gamma,e_{-\gamma}]=h_\gamma$, where $h_\gamma\in\mathfrak h$ is the coroot of $\gamma$, the element of $[\mathfrak g_\gamma,\mathfrak g_{-\gamma}]$ with $\gamma(h_\gamma)=2$ for the root spaces $\mathfrak g_{\pm\gamma}=\{x\in\mathfrak g:[h,x]=\pm\gamma(h)x\text{ for all }h\in\mathfrak h\}$, and for $\gamma+\delta\in R$ one has $[e_\gamma,e_\delta]=\pm(p_{\gamma,\delta}+1)e_{\gamma+\delta}$, where $p_{\gamma,\delta}=\max\{p\ge0:\delta-p\gamma\in R\}$; the bracket is zero if the sum is neither a root nor zero. Let $u,v\in R$ be distinct and not opposite. There is an ordering $(a,b)$ of $(u,v)$ for which the following assertions hold. The roots $a,b$ are linearly independent over $\mathbf Q$. Define $\operatorname{ad}(x)(y)=[x,y]$, $Y_k=(\operatorname{ad}e_a)^k(e_b)/k!$, and
$$p=\max\{i\geq0:b-ia\in R\},\qquad q=\max\{i\geq0:b+ia\in R\}.$$
Then $p+q\leq3$, $Y_0=e_b$, $Y_k=0$ for $k>q$, and for $0\leq k\leq q$ there is an integer $c_k$ with
$$Y_k=c_k e_{b+ka},\qquad |c_k|=\binom{p+k}{k}.$$
Every $[Y_i,Y_j]$ commutes in the Lie sense with every $Y_k$: $[[Y_i,Y_j],Y_k]=0$ for $0\leq i,j,k\leq q$. For $1\leq d\leq2q$ put
$$C_d=\frac12\sum_{\substack{0\leq i<j\leq q\\ i+j=d}}[Y_i,Y_j].$$
If $2b+da\notin R$, then $C_d=0$. Otherwise $C_d=z_d e_{2b+da}$ for some $z_d\in\mathbf Z$. Empty sums are zero. No assertion about divided powers in an enveloping algebra is part of this statement.

source.place: Appendix C, section g, rank-two classification, table (180) and the four diagrams, printed pp.621--622; Section 23h, Theorem 23.71, pp.508--509. Agent-stated local bracket/parity consequence of these sources, not a theorem explicitly stated there.

proof.text: Reducedness gives $R\cap\mathbf Qu=\{u,-u\}$, so distinct nonopposite $u,v$ are independent. Put $W=\mathbf Qu+\mathbf Qv$ and $S=R\cap W$. This is finite, spans $W$, excludes zero and remains reduced. For $r\in S$ restrict its coroot functional to $W$. The reflection $x\mapsto x-c_r(x)r$ preserves $W$ and $R$; it is an involution, so permutes $S$, and $c_r(S)\subseteq\mathbf Z$, $c_r(r)=2$. Thus $S$ satisfies the rank-two classification hypotheses. Every root membership test below involves vectors in $W$, so membership in $R$ is exactly membership in $S$.

source.place: Appendix C.12--C.18 and section g, table (180), four diagrams, printed pp.610--611,621--622; Theorem 23.71, printed pp.508--509. Agent calculation from the coordinate lists and the assumed Chevalley bracket normalization.

proof.text:
Apply [lem-sfb-rank-two-root-coordinate-classification] to $S\subset W$, using its basis $(s,t)$. For coordinates $(x,y)$ set $L=x^2+y^2$ in $A_1\times A_1$, $L=x^2-xy+y^2$ in $A_2$, $L=x^2-2xy+2y^2$ in $B_2$, and $L=x^2-3xy+3y^2$ in $G_2$. Choose $(a,b)$ from $(u,v)$ with $L(a)\le L(b)$; ties can be ordered either way. The following table is obtained by substituting the signed coordinate vectors of the four displayed sets into $b+ka$. It lists all possible $(p,q)$:
$$\begin{array}{c|l}
A_1\times A_1&(0,0)\\
A_2&(1,0),(0,1)\\
B_2&(0,0),(2,0),(0,2),(1,1)\\
G_2&(1,0),(3,0),(0,0),(0,1),(0,3),(2,1),(1,2).
\end{array}$$
For each pair the integers $k$ giving roots are exactly $-p,-p+1,\ldots,q$; hence $p+q\le3$. This is a finite membership calculation: run over all signed roots $a,b$, discard $b=\pm a$ and $L(a)>L(b)$, and compare the two integer coordinates of $b+ka$ with each signed vector in the relevant list. No conjugacy or transitivity of root pairs is being assumed.

source.place: Appendix C.12--C.18 and section g, table (180), four diagrams, printed pp.610--611,621--622; Theorem 23.71, printed pp.508--509. Agent calculation from the coordinate lists and the assumed Chevalley bracket normalization.

proof.text:
Write $r_k=b+ka$. The interval just computed gives $p_{a,r_k}=p+k$ for $0\le k<q$, since $r_k-ja=b+(k-j)a$. Thus the assumed Chevalley formula gives $[e_a,e_{r_k}]=\varepsilon_k(p+k+1)e_{r_{k+1}}$ with $\varepsilon_k\in\{1,-1\}$. Repeated substitution, starting from $Y_0=e_b$, yields
$$Y_k=\left(\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\varepsilon_j\right)\frac{(p+1)\cdots(p+k)}{k!}e_{r_k}=\left(\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\varepsilon_j\right)\binom{p+k}{k}e_{r_k}.$$
The coefficient is an integer of the required absolute value (empty products are one). Since $b+(q+1)a$ is neither a root nor zero, $[e_a,e_{r_q}]=0$. Hence $Y_{q+1}=0$ and all higher $Y_k$ vanish by applying $\operatorname{ad}e_a$ again.

source.place: Appendix C.12--C.18 and section g, table (180), four diagrams, printed pp.610--611,621--622; Theorem 23.71, printed pp.508--509. Agent calculation from the coordinate lists and the assumed Chevalley bracket normalization.

proof.text:
Continue the finite coordinate check from [lem-sfb-rank-two-root-coordinate-classification]. For $0\le i<j\le q$ the only cases in which $r_i+r_j=2b+(i+j)a$ is a root are the following:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
\text{type}&(p,q)&(i,j)&p_{r_i,r_j}&\text{root sum}\\
G_2&(0,3)&(0,3)&0&2b+3a\\
G_2&(0,3)&(1,2)&2&2b+3a\\
G_2&(1,2)&(0,1)&2&2b+a.
\end{array}$$
To compute the fourth column compare $r_j-hr_i$ with the same signed coordinate list for successive nonnegative $h$. For the first two rows, $3b+(3+k)a$ is absent for every $0\le k\le3$; for the last row, $3b+(1+k)a$ is absent for every $0\le k\le2$. These exclusions use the same two-coordinate comparison. Thus the table also records every possible nonzero bracket and the absence of every root obtained by adding a further $r_k$ to its weight. All these sums are nonzero by independence of $a,b$.

source.place: Appendix C.12--C.18 and section g, table (180), four diagrams, printed pp.610--611,621--622; Theorem 23.71, printed pp.508--509. Agent calculation from the coordinate lists and the assumed Chevalley bracket normalization.

proof.text: Bilinearity and the Chevalley zero-bracket rule show that all brackets omitted in step 4 vanish. Also $[Y_i,Y_i]=0$ by alternation and reversed pairs change the sign. For a listed pair its bracket is a scalar multiple of $e_{2b+(i+j)a}$, and the final exclusions in step 4 give $[[Y_i,Y_j],Y_k]=0$ for all $k$. This proves centrality. In particular all cases outside the two listed $G_2$ string types have $C_d=0$.

source.place: Appendix C.12--C.18 and section g, table (180), four diagrams, printed pp.610--611,621--622; Theorem 23.71, printed pp.508--509. Agent calculation from the coordinate lists and the assumed Chevalley bracket normalization.

proof.text: It remains to check integrality for the listed pairs; no compatibility of the Chevalley signs is needed. In the $(p,q)=(0,3)$ case, the absolute values of $(c_0,c_1,c_2,c_3)$ are $(1,1,1,1)$. The table and the Chevalley formula give bracket coefficients of absolute values $1$ for $(0,3)$ and $3$ for $(1,2)$. Both contribute only to $C_3$, whose coefficient is $(\pm1\pm3)/2\in\mathbf Z$. In the $(p,q)=(1,2)$ case the absolute values are $(1,2,3)$; the sole pair $(0,1)$ has bracket coefficient of absolute value $1\cdot2\cdot3=6$, so $C_1=\pm3e_{2b+a}$. Every other $C_d$ is zero. A sum whose weight $2b+da$ is not a root has no nonzero summand by step 4; no weight here is zero. These observations give the required integers $z_d$, with $z_d=0$ whenever the root exists but its bracket sum is empty or zero. If $q=0$, the range $1\le d\le2q$ is empty, as required.
